title: Old Testament prayer (CCC 2568–2589)
hook: Abraham listens, Moses intercedes, David praises, Elijah waits

segments.voice: Yesterday, what prayer is: gift, covenant, communion, and a stranger at a well asking for a drink. Your line was god thirsts that we thirst. Did you remember the well? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

Four people, four different places. An old man hearing his name called, and answering: here I am. A leader on a mountain, arguing with God for people who have just let him down. A king with a harp, singing. A prophet in a cave, worn out, waiting for a voice that isn't in the wind or the fire. In the Catechism, these four are among the teachers of prayer before Christ. Today: Old Testament prayer.
screen: `AN OLD MAN: HERE I AM.` → `A LEADER ON A MOUNTAIN.` → `A KING WITH A HARP.` → `A PROPHET IN A CAVE.`

segments.voice: Abraham first. The Catechism says his heart was in tune with God's will, and that his prayer showed first in deeds, not words: he went, as the Lord told him. When God calls, in the Douay-Rheims, Abraham answers, "Here I am." That's listening as prayer. Readiness. The Catechism also notes that he dared to plead for the city of Sodom: even the listener speaks up. Moses next. On the mountain, after the people made the golden calf, Moses stands between them and God and pleads for them. The Catechism calls this intercession, and it points out that Moses doesn't pray for himself. He prays for the very people who made his life hard. Exodus says the Lord spoke with Moses face to face, the way a man speaks to a friend. The Catechism draws from that: intercession grows out of friendship. Then David. The Catechism calls him the king after God's own heart, a shepherd who prays for his people and in their name. His prayer is praise and repentance, and tradition ties psalms to his name. Praise, in his hands, is music. Last, Elijah. On Mount Carmel he prays and fire comes down. But later he flees into the desert, exhausted, and on the mountain of God he waits. The Lord is not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire. Then comes what the Douay-Rheims calls "a whistling of a gentle air." That is where Elijah meets the Lord. Waiting is prayer too. Listen, intercede, praise, wait. Read together, they're lessons learned slowly. A long school, before the Gospels.
screen: `ABRAHAM: HERE I AM.` · `MOSES: PLEADING FOR OTHERS.` · `DAVID: PRAISE AS MUSIC.` · `ELIJAH: A GENTLE AIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray like one of them. Settle, and breathe. Choose one of the four. Abraham: just be ready, and if you pray, say here I am. Moses: hold someone who has let you down, and ask good for them. David: name one thing that deserves praise, and let it fill you. Elijah: do nothing at all, and wait for the quiet underneath the noise. Stay with the one you chose. If you don't pray, just take that posture, and see what it's like. The bell holds the time.
Old Testament prayer. In Catholic teaching, the long school of prayer before Christ: Abraham's readiness, Moses' pleading, David's praise, Elijah's waiting. Today's word.
Your line: the long school. Today, notice which of the four comes most naturally to you, and which one you've never tried. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: The Church prays the psalms each day in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Old Testament readings are heard at Mass; the Catechism presents Abraham, Moses, David and Elijah as teachers of prayer.

original.note: Hebrew: here I am — Abraham's answer when God calls him.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the Old Testament, prayer is mostly asking for things.
what it means: listening, interceding, praising and waiting, each taught by someone who lived it.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism reads the Old Testament as a school of prayer, from Abraham's obedience to Elijah's gentle air.

notes: CCC paraphrased throughout (copyrighted translation). Check: Abraham's heart attuned and first prayer as obedience, intercession for Sodom (2570–2571); Moses' intercession and friendship, face to face (2574–2577); David the king after God's heart, shepherd praying for his people (2579); Elijah at Carmel and Horeb (2582–2583).
'Here I am' attributed to Genesis 22:1; Abraham also answers this way at 22:11. Confirm Douay-Rheims wording.
Douay-Rheims 3 Kings 19:12 'a whistling of a gentle air': confirm exact wording.
'Tradition ties psalms to his name' stays with tradition rather than a count.
'The king after God's own heart' echoes 1 Samuel 13:14 / Acts 13:22 as used in CCC 2579.

Editor: hook miscount fixed ('here I am' is three words in English) and the unsourced tent setting, 'no prayer book' and 'school of prayer' attribution cut; Abraham's prayer now 'first in deeds' per CCC 2570; Elijah close no longer attributes an unchecked line to the CCC; howItsDone no longer says all Catholics pray the psalms daily.

Audit (1132–1141 pass): no changes. Genesis 22:1 and 3 Kings 19:12 (Douay-Rheims), Hebrew hinneni, Exodus 32:11–14 and 33:11, and CCC 2570–2583 (Abraham's prayer first in deeds, Moses praying for the people not himself, David 'after God's own heart', Elijah at Carmel and Horeb) checked and found accurate.
